Dear Sir/Madam, 
 
Subject:  
1. Notice of the 50th Annual General Meeting (“AGM”) and Integrated Annual Report for 
the Financial Year 2025-26 
2. Closure of Register of Members and Share Transfer Books 
 
In terms of Regulation 30 and 34 of the Securities and Exchange Board of India (Listing 
Obligations and Disclosure Requirements) Regulations, 2015, please find attached herewith the 
Notice of the 50th Annual General Meeting ("AGM") of the Company and the Fourth Integrated 
Annual Report of the Company for the Financial Year 2025-26 including the Business 
Responsibility and Sustainability Report. 
 
In accordance with the relevant circulars issued by Ministry of Corporate Affairs and Securities 
and Exchange Board of India the aforesaid documents are being dispatched electronically to 
those Members whose email IDs are registered with the Company / Depository Participants. 
 
The Notice of the AGM and Integrated Annual Report is also being uploaded on the Company's 
website and can be accessed at www.chini.com. 
 
Further, the register of Members and Share Transfer Books of the Company will remain closed 
from Thursday, 10th September, 2026 to Wednesday, 16th September, 2026 (both days 
inclusive) for the purpose of the 50th AGM of the Company. 
 
We request you to take the above information on record.  
 
Thanking you,  
 
Yours faithfully,  
For Balrampur Chini Mills Limited 
 
 
Manoj Agarwal  
Company Secretary & Compliance Officer

Notice
NOTICE is hereby given that the 50th (Fiftieth) Annual 
General Meeting (“AGM”) of the Members of Balrampur 
Chini Mills Limited (“ Company”) will be held on Wednesday, 
the 16th day of September, 2026 at 04:00 P.M. (IST) through 
Video Conferencing (“VC”) / Other Audio Visual Means 
(“OAVM”) to transact the following businesses:
Ordinary Business(s):
1. 	 To receive, consider and adopt the Audited Standalone 
Financial Statements of the Company for the Financial 
Year ended 31st March, 2026 and the Reports of the 
Board of Directors and Auditors’ thereon.
2. 	 To receive, consider and adopt the Audited 
Consolidated Financial Statements of the Company 
for the Financial Year ended 31st March, 2026 and the 
Report of the Auditors’ thereon.
3. 	 To approve and confirm the Interim Dividend of 
H3.50 (350%) per equity share, having face value of 
H1, as final dividend paid by the Company during the 
Financial Year ended 31st March, 2026.
4.	
To appoint a Director pursuant to Section 152(6) of the 
Companies Act, 2013, in place of Mr. Praveen Gupta 
(DIN: 09651564), who retires by rotation at this Annual 
General Meeting and being eligible, offers himself for 
re-appointment.
Special Business(s):

of

of Directors of the Company, consent of the Members 
be and is hereby accorded for re-appointment of 
Mr. Vivek Saraogi (DIN: 00221419) as the Chairman and

March, 2032 whose office shall not be liable to retire 
by rotation, on such terms and conditions including

vary, alter and modify the terms and conditions of 
re-appointment including designation, remuneration

prescribed in the Explanatory Statement and in 
accordance with the provisions of applicable laws.

the Company:

Section 148 and other applicable provisions, if any,

9.	
Approval for Acceptance of Grant Assistance 
from Biotechnology Industry Research Assistance 
Council (BIRAC).
To consider and if thought fit, to pass, with or without 
modification(s), the following resolution as an 
Ordinary Resolution:
“RESOLVED THAT pursuant to the applicable 
provisions of the Companies Act, 2013, the rules 
made thereunder, the Articles of Association of the 
Company and all other applicable laws, regulations, 
guidelines, notifications and approvals, as may be 
applicable (including any statutory modification(s) 
or re-enactment(s) thereof for the time being 
in force), and as required by the Biotechnology 
Industry Research Assistance Council (“BIRAC”), the 
consent of the Members of the Company be and 
is hereby accorded to accept the offer of BIRAC 
for Grant Assistance to the Company in the form 
of a Grant Letter Agreement (“GLA”), for an amount 
not exceeding H7500 Lakhs (Rupees Seventy-Five 
Crore only) on the terms and conditions set out in 
the standard form of GLA received from BIRAC and 
also avail disbursement(s) in part or in full from time 
to time as may be allowed by BIRAC under ‘
 
BioEnablers: Biofoundries and Biomanufacturing 
Hubs’, programme for implementation of the 
project titled “~100 t/a PLA Co-Polymer R&D Facility, 
having an aggregate project cost of H10975 Lakhs, 
comprising BIRAC assistance of H7500 Lakhs and the 
Company’s contribution of H3475 Lakhs on the terms 
and conditions contained in the GLA.
RESOLVED FURTHER THAT the following persons, viz 
Mr. Vivek Saraogi, Chairman and Managing Director; 
Ms. Avantika Saraogi, Executive Director; Mr. Praveen 
Gupta, Whole-time Director; Mr. Pramod Patwari, 
Chief Financial Officer; Mr. Rohit Bothra, President 
(Taxation & Strategy); Mr. Vinay Khanna, Sr. Vice 
President – Business Planning & Operations; Mr. Manoj 
Agarwal, Company Secretary; and Mr. Shivesh Kumar 
Singh, Chief Technology Officer of the Company be 
and are hereby severally authorised to convey BIRAC 
acceptance on behalf of the Company of the said 
offer for grant assistance on the terms and conditions 
contained in GLA referred to above and to execute 
such deeds, documents, and other writings as may 
be necessary or required for this purpose including 
all amendments therein as may be suggested by and 
acceptable to BIRAC from time to time.
RESOLVED FURTHER THAT the funds received 
by the Company from BIRAC shall strictly be used 
for the purpose and objectives set out in the Grant 
Letter Agreement.
RESOLVED FURTHER THAT the Company shall repay 
the fixed royalty (not less than 5% per year of the Grant) 
disbursed to the Company, within a period of five 
years, starting from the end of a two-year relaxation 
period (24 months) from the date of the first release 
of the grant assistance.
RESOLVED FURTHER THAT the Company has to pay 
the fixed royalty amount till it becomes equal to the 
total amount disbursed within a period of 5 years.
RESOLVED FURTHER THAT the Common Seal of the 
Company be affixed to:
a.	
the stamped engrossment(s) in duplicate of GLA;
b.	 the stamped engrossment(s) of other documents 
as may be required (Fixed Royalty Payment 
Schedule) to be executed under the Common 
Seal of the Company in favour of BIRAC to secure 
the aforesaid facilities in the presence of any one

NOTES:
1.	
An Explanatory Statement pursuant to Section 102 
of the Companies Act, 2013 (as amended) (“Act”) and 
Revised Secretarial Standard on General Meetings 
(“SS-2”), issued by the Institute of Company Secretaries 
of India (‘ICSI’) setting out the material facts relating to 
Special Businesses under Items 5, 6, 7, 8 and 9 of the 
Notice for convening the 50th Annual General Meeting 
(AGM/ Meeting) of the Company (“Notice”) which the 
Board of Directors have considered and decided to 
include as Special Business is annexed hereto. The 
said Statements also contain the recommendation 
of the Board of Directors of the Company in terms 
of Regulation 17(11) of the Securities and Exchange 
Board of India (Listing Obligations and Disclosure 
Requirements) Regulations, 2015 (as amended) 
(“Listing Regulations”). Additional disclosures, pursuant 
to the requirements of SS-2 and Regulation 36(3) of 
the Listing Regulations, in respect of the directors 
seeking appointment / re-appointment form part of 
this Notice.
2.	
Pursuant to the Circulars No. 14/2020 dated April 8, 
2020, No. 17/2020 dated April 13, 2020, No. 20/2020 
dated May 05, 2020, and subsequent circulars issued 
in this regard, the latest being General Circular No. 
03/2025 dated 22nd September, 2025 (prescribing 
the procedure and manner of conducting the AGM 
through VC/OAVM), (hereinafter collectively referred 
to as “MCA Circulars”), the Ministry of Corporate 
Affairs(“MCA”) has permitted companies to conduct 
their AGM through VC or OAVM.
3.	
In compliance with the applicable provisions of the Act, 
Listing Regulations, MCA Circulars and SEBI Circulars, 
the Board of Directors has approved conducting of 
the 50th AGM of the Company through VC/OAVM. 
The Registered Office of the Company shall be 
the deemed venue of the AGM. KFin Technologies 
Limited, the Registrar and Transfer Agent of the 
Company (“KFintech”or “RTA”), will provide facility for 
voting through remote e-voting, for participation in the 
AGM through VC/OAVM facility and e-voting during 
the AGM. Participation of the Members through VC / 
OAVM will be reckoned for the purpose of quorum for 
the AGM as per Section 103 of the Act.
4.	
Keeping the convenience of the Members positioned 
in different time zones, the Meeting has been 
scheduled at 04:00 P.M. (IST).
5.	
The Notice will be sent to those Members/ Beneficial 
Owners whose name appears in the Register of 
Members/ list of beneficiaries received from the 
Depositories as on Friday, 14th August, 2026.
6.	
IN TERMS OF THE MCA CIRCULARS AND SEBI 
CIRCULARS MENTIONED HEREIN ABOVE, THE 
REQUIREMENT OF SENDING PROXY FORMS TO 
HOLDERS OF SECURITIES AS PER PROVISIONS OF 
SECTION 105 OF THE ACT READ WITH REGULATION 
44(4) OF THE LISTING REGULATIONS, HAS BEEN 
DISPENSED WITH. THEREFORE, THE FACILITY TO 
APPOINT PROXY BY THE MEMBERS WILL NOT BE 
AVAILABLE FOR THIS AGM AND CONSEQUENTLY, 
THE PROXY FORM, ATTENDANCE SLIP INCLUDING 
ROUTE MAP ARE NOT ANNEXED TO THE NOTICE.
However, in pursuance of Section 113 of the Act and 
Rules made thereunder, the institutional/ corporate 
members are entitled to appoint their authorised 
representatives for the purpose of voting through 
remote e-voting or for the participation and e-voting 
during the AGM, through VC or OAVM. In this regard, 
they are required to send scanned copy (PDF / 
JPG Format) of the relevant Board Resolution or by 
resolution of other governing body, authorising their 
representative to vote on their behalf, to the Scrutinizer 
through e-mail at cs.amberahmad@gmail.com with 
the subject line “Balrampur Chini Mills Limited – 50th 
AGM” with a copy marked to evoting@kfintech.com 
and investorgrievances@bcml.in.

ANNUAL

7.	
In compliance with the aforesaid MCA and SEBI 
Circulars, regulation 36 of Listing Regulations and any 
other relevant laws made thereunder, the Notice of 
the 50th AGM and the Integrated Annual Report for 
the FY 25-26 is being sent only through electronic 
mode to all the Members whose email addresses are 
registered with the Company/RTA/ Depositories. For 
the members whose email IDs are not registered with 
the Company / RTA / Depositories, a letter providing 
the web-link including the exact path, where 
complete details of the annual report is available 
shall be sent to those members in compliance of 
regulation 36(1)(b) of SEBI (Listing Obligations and 
Disclosure Requirements) Regulations, 2015. Further, 
the hard copies of the annual report will be sent to 
those members who request for the same.
8.	
Members may note that the Notice of the 50th AGM 
and the Integrated Annual Report for the FY 25-26, 
will also be available on the Company’s website at 
www.chini.com, websites of the Stock Exchanges, 
i.e. BSE Limited and National Stock Exchange of India

Limited at www.bseindia.com and www.nseindia.
com respectively, and on the website of the e-voting 
agency https://evoting.kfintech.com/.
9.	
Pursuant to the MCA’s Circular, the Company shall 
publish a newspaper advertisement specifying that 
the Company intends to convene a general meeting 
through VC / OAVM in compliance with applicable 
provisions of the Act read with the MCA Circulars, and 
for the said purpose it proposes to send notices to all 
its members by e-mail. However, Members who have 
still not registered their email IDs, are requested to do 
so at the earliest, in the following manner:
a) 	 Members holding shares in electronic mode can 
get their email IDs registered by contacting their 
respective Depository Participant.
b) 	 Members holding shares in physical mode are 
requested to register their email IDs with the 
Company or Kfintech, for receiving the Notice 
and Integrated Annual Report. Requests can 
be emailed to einward.ris@kfintech.com or 
secretarial@bcml.in / investorgrievances@bcml.in
The Members are urged to support the Green Initiative 
of the Government of India by choosing to receive the 
communication from the Company through email.
PROCEDURE 
FOR 
JOINING 
THE 
AGM 
THROUGH VC / OAVM:
10.	 Members will be able to attend the AGM through VC / 
OAVM of the AGM at https://emeetings.kfintech.com 
by using their remote e-voting login credentials and 
selecting the ‘Event’ for Company’s AGM.
	
Members who do not have the User ID and Password 
for e-voting or have forgotten the User ID and 
Password may retrieve the same by following the 
remote e-voting instructions mentioned in the Notice.
11.	 Members may join the AGM through Laptops, 
Smartphones, Tablets or iPads for better experience. 
Further, Members will be required to use the internet 
with a good speed to avoid any disturbance during 
the AGM. Members will need the latest version of 
Chrome, Safari, MS Edge or Mozilla Firefox.
Please note that participants connecting from Mobile 
Devices or Tablets or through Laptops connecting via 
mobile hotspot may experience Audio / Video loss 
due to fluctuation in their respective network. It is 
therefore recommended to use stable Wi-Fi or LAN 
connection to mitigate any glitches.
Members will be required to grant access to the web- 
cam to enable two-way video conferencing.
12.	 The facility of joining the AGM through VC / OAVM 
shall open 30 minutes before the time scheduled for 
the AGM and shall be kept open throughout the AGM. 
1000 Members will be able to participate in the AGM 
through VC / OAVM on a first come - first-serve basis.
Large Members (i.e. Members holding 2% or 
more 
shareholding), 
promoters, 
institutional 
investors, directors, key managerial personnel, the 
Chairpersons of the Audit Committee, Nomination 
and Remuneration Committee and Stakeholders 
Relationship Committee, Auditors, etc. will not be 
subject to the aforesaid restriction of first-come-first 
serve basis.
13.	 Institutional Members are encouraged to participate 
at the AGM through VC / OAVM and vote thereat.
14.	 Members, holding shares as on the cut-off date i.e. 
Wednesday, 9th September, 2026 and who would 
like to speak or express their views or ask questions 
during the AGM may register themselves as speakers 
at https://emeetings.kfintech.com and clicking on 
‘Speaker Registration’ on Monday, 14th September, 
2026 (11:00 A.M. IST to 5:00 P.M. IST). Those Members 
who have registered themselves as a speaker will 
only be allowed to speak / express their views / ask 
questions during the AGM. The Company at the 
discretion of the Chairman, reserves the right to 
restrict the number of speakers depending on the 
availability of time at the AGM. Selection of Speakers 
would be made considering representation from 
different geographies/ diverse categories/professions/ 
age profiles and using random selection method. In 
view of smooth conducting of the AGM each speaker 
is requested to express their views in 2 minutes.
Alternatively, Members holding shares as on the cut- 
off date may also visit https://emeetings.kfintech.com 
and click on the tab ‘Post Your Queries’ and post their 
queries/views/questions in the window provided, by 
mentioning their name, demat account number/
folio number, email ID and mobile number. The 
window will close at 5.00 P.M. (IST) on Monday, 14th 
September, 2026.
15.	 Members who need assistance before or during the 
AGM with use of technology, can contact Kfintech at 
1-800-309-4001 or write to them at evoting@kfintech.
com.

PROCEDURE FOR REMOTE E-VOTING AND 
VOTING DURING THE AGM:
16.	 In accordance with the provisions of Section 108 
and other applicable provisions, if any, of the Act, 
read with Rule 20 of the Companies (Management 
and Administration) Rules, 2014 and amendments 
thereto and Regulation 44 of the Listing Regulations, 
the Company has engaged the services of Kfintech to 
provide remote e-voting facility to all the Members to 
enable them to cast their votes electronically in respect 
of the business to be transacted at the Meeting.
17.	 Members are requested to attend and participate in 
the ensuing AGM through VC / OAVM and cast their 
vote either through remote e-voting facility or through 
e-voting facility to be provided during the AGM.
18.	 In case of any query and / or help, in respect of attending 
the AGM through VC/ OAVM mode, Members may 
refer to the Help & Frequently Asked Questions 
(FAQs) and ‘AGM VC/ OAVM’ user manual available 
at the download Section of https://evoting.kfintech.
com/ or contact Mr. Sashidhar Mannava, Deputy Vice 
President - Corporate Registry or Mr. Balaji S Reddy, 
Senior Manager – Corporate Registry of Kfintech at 
the email ID at evoting@kfintech.com, Kfintech’s toll 
free no.: 1800-309-4001 for any further clarifications / 
technical assistance that may be required.
19.	 The process and manner for remote e-voting are as 
under:	
a)	
Pursuant to the provisions of Rule 20 of the 
Companies (Management and Administration) 
Rules, 2014 (as amended), the SS-2 and 
Regulation 44 of the Listing Regulations read with 
MCA Circulars and SEBI Circulars, the Company 
is pleased to provide remote e-voting facility 
to its Members in respect of the business to be 
transacted during the AGM and facility for those 
Members participating in the AGM to cast vote 
through e-voting system during the AGM.
b)	 The facility for voting shall also be made available 
during the AGM and the Members participating 
in the Meeting who have not casted their votes 
by remote e-voting shall be able to exercise their 
right during the Meeting through e-voting.
c)	 The Members who have casted their vote by 
remote e-voting prior to the AGM may also 
participate in the AGM but shall not be entitled to 
cast their vote again.
d)	 The facility of casting the votes by the Members 
using an electronic voting system (“remote 
e-voting”) during the prescribed time prior to 
AGM and voting during AGM will be provided by 
service provider Kfintech.
e)	 The remote e-voting period commences on 
Sunday, 13th September, 2026 (10:00 A.M. IST) 
and ends on Tuesday, 15th September, 2026 (5:00 
P.M. IST). During this period Members of the 
Company, holding shares either in physical form 
or in dematerialized form, as on the cut-off date

Mr. Vivek Saraogi is a dynamic industrialist and an eminent leader in the Indian sugar industry, with over four 
decades of experience. As the Chairman and Managing Director of the Company, he has played a pivotal role 
in transforming the Company into one of the most efficient and diversified integrated sugar manufacturing

Under his visionary leadership, the Company, which commenced operations in 1975 with a single sugar unit 
at Balrampur, has expanded significantly and today operates 10 sugar manufacturing units with a combined 
crushing capacity of 80,000 tonnes of cane per day. The Company also operates 10 co-generation power plants 
with a combined saleable capacity of 175.7 MW and 5 distillery units with a combined production capacity of 
1,050 KL per day and its upcoming Poly Lactic Acid (PLA) plant will manufacture 80,000 tonnes of PLA per year.
Through a combination of strategic foresight, operational excellence, and sustained focus on growth through 
both organic and inorganic expansion, Mr. Vivek Saraogi has successfully steered the Company to a leadership 
position in the Indian sugar industry. His emphasis on innovation, efficiency enhancement, sustainability, and 
value creation has significantly strengthened the Company’s operational and financial performance over 
the years.
Considering the dynamic business environment and the evolving opportunities in the sugar, ethanol, green 
energy, and bio-based products sectors, there is a continuous need to formulate and review business strategies 
for effective implementation and long-term growth. This requires Mr. Vivek Saraogi’s continued guidance, 
strategic direction, and active involvement in managing the overall affairs and operations of the Company.

Founded in 1975, Balrampur Chini 
Mills Limited ranks among the 
country’s most extensive integrated 
private sugar enterprises. The 
organisation is helmed by Mr. Vivek 
Saraogi and strengthened by an 
experienced leadership team.
The Company’s creditworthiness was 
reaffirmed with a long-term credit 
rating of AA+ with stable outlook 
and a short-term rating of A1+ by 
CRISIL. India Ratings re-affirmed the 
Company’s long-term credit rating 
of Ind AA+ with Stable outlook and a 
short-term rating of Ind A1+.
Balrampur’s workforce consists 
of experienced professionals 
spanning the agriculture, IT, finance, 
manufacturing and ESG functions. As 
on 31st March, 2026, the Company 
employed 5,985 individuals, with 
~ 80% having worked with the 
Company for five years or longer.
The Company is set to achieve 
the Bonsucro Certification for 
the Kumbhi Unit. Strong focus on 
hygiene and sanitation enabled 
the Mankapur, Rauzagaon and 
Kumbhi units to secure FSSC 
22000 certification. In addition, 
the Company was granted ISO 
14001:2015 for its environmental 
management system and ISO 
45001:2018 for its occupational 
health and safety framework.
The Company’s operations span 
sugar manufacturing, ethanol 
production and the co-generation of 
power. In FY 25-26, sugar accounted 
for 75.79% of overall revenues, while 
the distillery segment contributed 
23.69%.
Balrampur’s shares remained actively 
traded on the BSE (code: 500038) 
and NSE (code: BALRAMCHIN). As 
on 31st March, 2026, the Company’s 
market value stood at H10,038.96 
crore, while the Company’s 
promoters held 42.85% of the equity.
The Company continued to 
emphasise ecological responsibility 
by directing capital towards 
improved waste treatment, lowering 
water usage, recycling effluents 
and finding productive applications 
of by-products. It also initiated the 
development of poly lactic acid, a 
bio-based plastic alternative.
Based in Kolkata, the Company 
runs ten sugar mills situated across 
the cane-abundant regions of 
Eastern and Central Uttar Pradesh. 
These locations also include five 
distilleries and ten cogeneration 
plants, forming one of the industry’s 
most integrated capacities. The units 
operate in Balrampur, Babhnan, 
Tulsipur, Akbarpur, Gularia, Maizapur, 
Mankapur, Rauzagaon, Haidergarh 
and Kumbhi.

The Balrampur facility began operations with an initial 
crushing capacity of 800 TCD, which was later scaled to 
12,500 TCD. Its cogeneration plant has since grown to a 
capacity of 53.05 MW.
The Company secured a controlling interest in Babhnan 
Sugar Mill Limited, which operated with a 1,000 TCD 
crushing capacity at the time. This was increased to 
2,500 TCD by 1992–93 and later scaled to 10,000 TCD. 
Babhnan Sugar Mills Limited was formally amalgamated 
with BCML with effect from 1st April, 1994.
A distillery was commissioned at the Balrampur 
facility with an initial capacity of 60 KLPD. This was 
subsequently raised to 160 KLPD and thereafter to 330 
KLPD.
A controlling stake was acquired in Tulsipur Sugar 
Company Limited, situated close to Balrampur in 
Eastern Uttar Pradesh, which began with a crushing 
capacity of 2,500 TCD. The entity was merged into 
BCML from 1st April, 1999, after which its crushing 
capacity was upgraded to 7,000 TCD and cogeneration 
capacity enhanced to 9.0 MW.
Under an indenture of conveyance, Balrampur 
Commercial Enterprises Limited (BECL) transferred 
its land, buildings, assets and the entire sugar mill 
workforce to Balrampur Chini Mills Limited (BCML), after 
which BCML was no longer a subsidiary of BECL.
BCML’s equity shares were listed on the Calcutta 
Stock Exchange (CSE). Over a period of time, BCML’s 
equity shares were also listed on the BSE Ltd. (BSE) and 
National Stock Exchange of India Ltd. (NSE).

A new integrated sugar complex was set up at 
Haidergarh, beginning with a crushing capacity of 4,000 
TCD and a 20.25 MW bagasse-based cogeneration 
plant. These capacities were later upgraded to 5,000 
TCD and 23.25 MW.
The Company commissioned a 60 KLPD distillery at 
Babhnan, which was later scaled to 100 KLPD. The 
Babhnan unit also saw the installation of a cogeneration 
facility, initially 3 MW and subsequently expanded to 
27.76 MW.
The Company took over an integrated sugar facility 
at Rauzagaon from Dhampur Sugar Mills Ltd. At the 
time of acquisition, the unit operated with a crushing 
capacity of 7,500 TCD and 12 MW of power generation. 
These capacities were later increased to 8,000 TCD and 
25.75 MW.
BCML also acquired a 53.96% shareholding in Indo 
Gulf Industries Limited (IGIL), which ran a sugar mill at 
Maizapur with a crushing capacity of 3,000 TCD. After 
the sugar division was carved out of IGIL and merged 
with BCML, the Company divested its entire stake in 
IGIL in 2017. Post-integration, the crushing capacity at 
the Maizapur unit was raised to 4,000 TCD, along with 
the installation of a 10 MW cogeneration plant.
A greenfield integrated sugar complex was launched at 
Akbarpur with an initial crushing capacity of 7,000 TCD 
and an 18 MW bagasse-based co-generation plant. The 
crushing capacity was later raised to 7,500 TCD.
The Company developed another greenfield integrated 
sugar complex at Mankapur featuring 8,000 TCD 
of cane crushing capacity, a 34 MW bagasse-based 
cogeneration plant and a 100 KLPD distillery. The 
cogeneration capacity was later expanded to 43.60 MW.
A greenfield facility at Kumbhi was commissioned 
with an 8,000 TCD crushing capacity and a 20 MW 
cogeneration plant. These capacities were subsequently 
increased to 10,000 TCD and 32.70 MW, respectively.
During the same year, another greenfield integrated 
sugar complex was set up in Gularia with 8,000 TCD 
crushing capacity and a 31.3 MW bagasse-based 
cogeneration unit, which was later upgraded to 38.86 
MW.

The Company installed incinerator systems across its 
distillery operations to achieve zero liquid discharge, 
which allowed production to be extended by nearly 
60 additional days each year, subject to feedstock 
availability.
Across ten-year period, the Company undertook six 
share buybacks, resulting in a total outlay of H1,009.49 
crore (including H110.73 crore in taxes). This was 
complemented by cumulative dividend payouts of 
H655.20 crore, inclusive of H52.46 crore in dividend 
distribution tax.
A 160 KLPD distillery was set up at Gularia, later scaled 
up to 200 KLPD.
The Company commissioned its fifth distillery at 
Maizapur, with an installed capacity of 320 KLPD.
Together, the distillery capacities now position the 
Company among the largest distillery operators within 
the Uttar Pradesh sugar sector.
The Company also initiated the implementation of a 
poly lactic acid manufacturing facility, with operations 
expected to commence in the second half of FY 26-27.

Strategic inflection: 
Resilience in a volatile global 
landscape
The 2025-26 fiscal year was a 
period of structural realignment. 
The Company navigated a complex 
nexus where domestic policy intent 
met global geopolitical instability. 
While our foundation remained 
anchored in agricultural strength, we 
decisively pivoted towards a future 
defined by sustainable materials and 
energy security.
Policy alignment and the 
ethanol imperative
India’s ethanol blending programme 
transitioned from an ambitious 
environmental target to a strategic 
sovereign asset. Designed to reduce 
crude oil imports, enhance energy 
security, improve farmer incomes, 
and lower vehicular emissions, the 
programme was characterised by 
strong policy, time-bound blending 
targets, and structured procurement 
mechanisms. However, there was 
no revision in B-heavy and juice 
based ethanol prices over three 
years, on the contrary, there was a 
lower offtake allocation to the sugar 
industry with a preference provided 
to maize-based ethanol providers, 
which represented a setback for 
those who had invested based on 
the government’s long-term policy.
In the face of the ongoing West 
Asia conflict, which saw the Strait of 
Hormuz - transit point for substantial 
part of India’s crude imports - 
effectively closed as of March 2026, 
domestic ethanol production served 
as a critical buffer against global 
energy shocks. The escalation of 
hostilities in West Asia (Iran-Israel-
US) introduced several ‘Black Swan’ 
variables into the 2026 agricultural 
economy. Brent crude volatility and 
the closure of the Strait of Hormuz 
doubled freight rates and spiked 
insurance premiums for Indian trade. 
Indian exports to traditional markets 
like Iran and the wider Gulf slowed 
significantly due to the inability to 
secure vessel insurance and the 
suspension of banking channels.
The conflict triggered a ‘fertilizer 
shock’. India, which sources nearly 
20% of its fertilizers from the Gulf, 
faced a significant surge in the cost 
of crop protection chemicals and 
urea. The Indian Rupee breached 
H95/USD, inflating the cost of 
imported agricultural inputs even 
as it theoretically improved export 
competitiveness.
The rapid progress towards 
higher ethanol blending ratios 
of up to 20% — achieved in a 
compressed timeframe — was 
underpinned by a combination 
of fiscal incentives, administered 
pricing clarity (since encountered 
interrupted encouragement) and 
offtake arrangements. For capital-
intensive industries such as cane-
based ethanol manufacturing, such 
visibility was essential. Investments 
in distillation capacity, feedstock 
linkages, storage infrastructure, 
and working capital had been 
undertaken with multi-year horizons 
and typically financed with debt. 
Consequently, alignment between 
input cost structures and output 
pricing mechanisms became central 
to long-term sustainability.
In the last three years, the 
Government approved increases 
in the Fair and Remunerative Price 
(FRP) of sugarcane by around 16.4%, 
reinforcing its commitment to farmer 
welfare and rural income stability. 
This measure strengthened the 
agricultural foundation of the ethanol 
value chain as well. However, 
during the same period, ethanol 
procurement prices were not revised 
upward. For cane-based ethanol 
manufacturers, this resulted in a

compression of operating spreads,

It is important to recognise that 
public policy operates within 
multiple, sometimes competing 
objectives - consumer price 
stability, fiscal prudence, inflation 
management, farmer welfare, and 
energy transition commitments. 
Decisions regarding administered 
pricing therefore reflected a broader 
macroeconomic balancing act. 
Nonetheless, from an industry 
perspective, the episode was 
noteworthy because it represented 
a shift from the earlier framework in 
which feedstock cost adjustments 
and ethanol pricing revisions were 
more visibly aligned.
For investors and business, the issue 
was less about a single pricing cycle 
and more about policy predictability. 
Capital formation in regulated or 
semi-regulated sectors is influenced 
by the credibility of signalling. When 
input costs are directly influenced 
by public policy while output pricing 
remains administratively determined, 
the synchronisation of the two 
becomes critical for sustaining 
investment confidence.
The ethanol sector witnessed 
significant capacity creation in 
the past five years, much of it 
supported by debt financing and 
predicated on blending targets 
that extended toward medium-
term milestones. Manufacturers 
made investment decisions based 
on an implicit understanding that 
policy consistency would support 
viable economics across cycles. A 
divergence, even when temporary, 
between feedstock price escalation 
and output pricing adjustment 
introduced a new variable into capital 
planning models.
This may not imply a structural 
policy reversal. Governments often 
recalibrate instruments in response 
to fiscal pressures, inflationary trends, 
or broader economic conditions. 
However, it does highlight the 
importance of transparent cost-
pass-through mechanisms in sectors 
where inputs and outputs are 
influenced by policy.
In sectors such as renewable energy, 
infrastructure, and biofuels, long-
term capital flows depend less on 
peak profitability and more on the 
stability of the rules governing the 
system. Investors, lenders, and 
strategic partners evaluate not 
only existing margins but also the 
resilience of policy architecture 
under stress. Even a short-term 
misalignment can influence risk 
perception, particularly for new 
entrants or incremental capacity 
investments.
From a systemic standpoint, the 
ethanol blending programme 
remained strategically important 
to India’s energy security and 
decarbonisation pathway. The long-
term direction of policy continued 
to be supportive of domestic biofuel 
production. However, the recent 
episode underscored the value of 
predictable adjustment frameworks 
- especially where government 
decisions directly influenced cost 
and revenue components of the 
value chain.
For industry participants, this 
experience reinforced the 
importance of Balance Sheet 
strength, operational efficiency, 
and diversification. Companies that 
maintained prudent leverage, strong 
liquidity buffers, and cost discipline 
remained positioned to absorb 
temporary policy-induced spread 
compression. It also highlighted 
the need for an ongoing dialogue 
between industry stakeholders 
and policymakers to ensure that 
implementation dynamics remained 
aligned with long-term objectives.
Viewed constructively, the episode 
may catalyse a more structured 
approach to pricing alignment 
mechanisms in the future. A 
transparent formula linking 
feedstock cost revisions and ethanol 
procurement pricing - subject to 
annual review - could strengthen 
investor confidence and sector 
sustainability without compromising 
broader macroeconomic priorities.
India’s energy transition journey 
remained one of the most ambitious 
globally. For it to continue attracting 
patient capital, policy consistency 
and clarity will remain as important 
as policy intent. The ethanol sector’s 
experience over the past years serves 
as a reminder that durable transitions 
are built not only on vision and 
targets, but also on the credibility of 
the mechanisms that sustain them.

soil health and organic carbon levels.

industrial growth and agricultural 
sustainability reinforce each other.

alternatives, which enhances PLA’s 
long-term competitiveness.

Environmental stewardship
Building a data-driven 
decarbonisation pathway
Climate change is no longer a 
distant environmental concern. It is 
increasingly influencing agricultural 
productivity, water availability, energy 
systems and business resilience 
across the world.
For a company where the value 
chain begins with agriculture, the 
implications are real. Changes in 
rainfall patterns, rising temperatures 
and growing pressure on natural 
resources affect the ecosystems 
that support farmers, operations and 
growth.
This reality reinforced a simple 
conviction at BCML: environmental 
responsibility cannot be driven 
by aspiration alone. It must be 
supported by data, measurement 
and disciplined action.
Before organisations can reduce 
emissions, they must first understand 
them. Before they can establish 
credible climate commitments, they 
must build a clear picture of where 
they stand today.
This belief guided our environmental 
strategy over the years.
For three consecutive years, 
BCML undertook comprehensive 
greenhouse gas inventorisation 
exercises, creating a robust 
understanding of our emissions 
footprint and enabling us to identify 
meaningful opportunities for 
decarbonisation. These assessments 
provided valuable insights into where 
improvements could be made, 
where investments could generate 
the greatest impact and how we 
could build a practical pathway 
towards a lower-carbon future. The 
result is a sustainability roadmap 
grounded in evidence rather than 
assumptions.
Our aspirations to achieve carbon 
neutrality by 2047 and net-zero 
emissions by 2055 are supported 
by measurable baselines, defined 
pathways and continuous 
performance monitoring. We 
expanded our assessment framework 
beyond conventional reporting 
requirements through Scope 3 
emissions evaluations and Life Cycle 
Assessments covering sugar, ethanol 
and sugarcane. These initiatives 
provide a deeper visibility into value-
chain impacts and help strengthen 
climate-related decision-making.
However, environmental stewardship 
extended beyond emissions.
Water conservation, resource 
efficiency, waste management 
and biodiversity protection 
remained important pillars of our 
environmental agenda. Through 
responsible water management, 
recycling initiatives, plantation 
programmes and continuous 
operational improvements, 
we worked to strengthen the 
environmental resilience of our 
operations and the communities that 
depended upon them.
The journey towards sustainability is 
long. But every meaningful journey 
began with understanding where 
one was, measuring progress and 
remaining committed to continuous 
improvement. That philosophy 
continued to guide BCML’s 
environmental stewardship efforts.

Mr. Vivek Saraogi, Chairman and Managing Director
Mr. Vivek Saraogi, a seasoned business leader, has long been recognized as a prominent 
figure in India’s sugar sector. Early in his career, he became one of the youngest individuals 
to head the Indian Sugar Mills Association. He has also chaired the Indian Sugar Exim 
Corporation Limited and previously contributed to FICCI and the Indian Chamber of 
Commerce, Kolkata, as a committee member. Under his stewardship, the Company has 
expanded significantly (both organic and inorganic), establishing itself as a leader within the 
industry. He holds a commerce degree from St. Xavier’s College, Kolkata.
Dr. Indu Bhushan, Lead Independent Director
Dr. Indu Bhushan, a former officer of the Indian Administrative Service (1983), is an 
accomplished technocrat and policy leader. He graduated in Electrical Engineering from IIT-
BHU and completed a postgraduate diploma in Control Systems and Instrumentation from 
IIT Delhi. He also holds a Ph.D. in Health Economics and a Master of Health Sciences from 
Johns Hopkins University, USA, and is a Chartered Financial Analyst (CFA).Dr. Bhushan has 
held pivotal leadership roles, including serving as the Chief Executive Officer of the National 
Health Authority and heading the Ayushman Bharat – Pradhan Mantri Jan Arogya Yojana . 
After nine years in the IAS, he worked as Senior Economist at the World Bank before joining 
the Asian Development Bank (ADB) in 1997. He later became Director-General of ADB’s 
Strategy and Policy Department, guiding the bank’s work across several Asian countries, 
including the People’s Republic of China. His oversight extended across sectors such as 
energy, environment, natural resources, transport, agriculture, public management, finance, 
regional cooperation, and urban-social development.
Mr. Chandra Kishore Mishra, Independent Director
Mr. Chandra Kishore Mishra has had an illustrious public service career of over 37 years in 
the Indian Administrative Service (1983 batch)with key leadership roles at both the state 
and central levels. He served as Secretary in the Ministry of Health & Family Welfare and 
concurrently held charge of the Ministry of AYUSH. Earlier, as Additional Secretary and 
Mission Director of the National Health Mission, he directed one of the largest public

Initiatives undertaken, 
FY 25-26
Environmental governance: 
Implementation of an environment 
tracker across all units ensured 
compliance with environmental 
clearances, air, water, and 
hazardous waste authorisations, and 
groundwater regulations. This was 
supported by periodic validation 
by the corporate technical team 
during plant visits, along with the 
presence of dedicated environment 
management cells at each unit for 
continuous oversight.
Water stewardship: Gap audits 
aligned with Sugar Charter 2.0 were 
conducted across all units, alongside 
a two-phase ETP augmentation 
programme, with Phase 1 completed 
at Balrampur, Mankapur, and 
Gularia, and Phase 2 planned for the 
remaining units during the off season 
in 2026.
Emission management: CCTV-
based monitoring was implemented 
across 25 boiler chimneys in sugar 
and distillery units, with a real-time 
remote access provided to our plant 
teams and the corporate technical 
team, enabling an immediate 
corrective action through central 
oversight.
Efficiency and technology 
upgrades: An investment of 
approximately H20 crore was made 
in boiler efficiency enhancement at 
Kumbhi, improving steam generation 
efficiency from 2.4 to 2.65 tonnes 
per tonne of bagasse and reducing 
fuel consumption cum emission 
intensity.
Advanced pollution control: The 
Company invested in wet ESP 
technology at Kumbhi, a first of its 
kind within the Company, along with 
the upgradation of wet scrubber 
systems aligned with operational 
requirements, strengthening 
emission control infrastructure 
across units.
Climate and weather intelligence: 
Rain gauges were replaced with IMD-
grade IS 5225 compliant equipment, 
and an automatic weather 
station was installed at Tulsipur in 
collaboration with IMD Lucknow, 
with plans to deploy automatic 
agricultural weather stations to 
support climate-linked decision 
making.
Circular and low carbon transition: 
Digital farmer engagement was 
driven through the Balram App for 
real-time advisory and information 
dissemination, while over 50% of 
crushing capacity was converted 
to sulphur-free sugar production. 
Waste valorisation initiatives included 
the conversion of boiler ash into 
potash-rich granules and utilisation 
of filter cake for bio manure and 
compressed biogas.
Biofuel expansion: Ethanol 
production capacity was significantly 
scaled up from 360 KLPD in 2017–18 
to 1,050 KLPD, contributing to 
India’s ethanol blending programme, 
reducing fossil fuel dependence, and 
enhancing the renewable energy 
footprint.
Air pollution control: ESP upgrades 
have been taken up at multiple units 
including Akbarpur, Balrampur and 
Mankapur along with Wet scrubbers 
enhancement at Balrampur, Babhnan 
and Rauzagaon and installation of 
next-generation ESPs at incineration 
boilers in Maizapur, Balrampur and 
Gularia. As a result, the average 
Suspended Particulate Matter (SPM) 
level recorded at these units is 45.86 
mg/Nm³, which is significantly lower 
than the permissible limits.
Efficiency gains: Continuous 
improvements in boiler efficiency 
led to reduced fuel consumption per 
tonne of steam and lowered stack 
emission intensity across operations.

to evolving regulatory and climate-

Life Cycle Assessment (LCA)
Overview
Life Cycle Assessment (LCA), also 
known as life cycle analysis, is a 
comprehensive methodology used 
to evaluate the environmental 
impacts associated with a product, 
process or service throughout its life 
cycle. 
Each stage of a product’s life 
cycle from the extraction of raw 
materials and manufacturing to its 
use and end-of-life management 
can contribute to a range of 
environmental impacts. 
These stages collectively constitute 
the life cycle of a product. LCA 
enables a holistic assessment of 
environmental impacts across the 
entire value chain, covering stages 
from the initial phase through the 
end of the product’s life cycle.
Life Cycle Assessment involves 
the systematic identification and 
evaluation of the inputs, outputs and 
potential environmental impacts 
associated with each stage of a 
product system’s life cycle.
LCA provides a comprehensive 
framework for assessing the 
environmental footprint of a 
product, considering its entire life 
span, from the resource extraction 
to end-of-life disposal.
The environmental impacts arising 
across different stages of a product 
or product system are quantified 
through the widely recognised 
Life Cycle Assessment (LCA) 
methodology. In this context, a 
product system may encompass a 
product, service, process or other 
related activities.
The ISO 14040 series is widely 
recognised as the standard for 
life cycle assessment. This series 
includes ISO 14040:2006, and 
ISO 14044:2006, and serves 
as a comprehensive guide for 
conducting LCA.
According to ISO 14040, LCA 
consists of four integral steps, 
offering a structured approach to 
assess the environmental aspects of 
products, services, and processes.
The first step: Goal and Scope 
Definition, involves establishing the 
primary objective of the LCA study 
and characterising the system under 
the analysis.
The second step: Life Cycle 
Inventory (LCI), consists of 
quantifying the inputs (e.g., Input 
materials, transportation, electricity 
data) and outputs (e.g., emissions 
and solid waste).
The third step: Life Cycle Impact 
Assessment (LCIA) calculates the 
environmental impacts of the 
studied system by converting the 
inventory data collected in the 
previous step into meaningful 
environmental impacts.
The fourth step : The interpretation 
phase involves the analysis and 
interpretation of the results 
obtained from the three preceding 
steps. This final step ensures 
comprehensive understanding 
and meaningful application of the 
insights got throughout the life cycle 
assessment.
A complete Life Cycle Assessment 
includes a definition of the goal 
and scope, an inventory analysis, 
an impact assessment, and an 
interpretation of results, providing a 
holistic understanding of a product’s 
environmental implications.
The Company has been conducting 
LCA since FY 23-24, a Leadership

Overview
Manufactured Capital represents 
the physical and technological 
backbone of an organisation — its 
plants, machinery, infrastructure, 
utilities, and production systems. 
It is the engine through which raw 
materials are transformed into 
marketable products, making it 
central to operational continuity, cost 
efficiency, and value creation.
An optimised manufacturing base 
generates a higher throughput, 
superior product quality, reduced 
resource consumption, and 
improved margins. It supports 
sustainability goals through energy 
efficiency, water conservation, and 
waste minimisation. 
Besides, Manufactured Capital 
increasingly reflects the integration 
of automation, digital monitoring, 
process innovation, and 
sustainability-led technologies.
At Balrampur Chini Mills Limited, 
Manufactured Capital is a dynamic 
and evolving capability. As one of 
India’s leading integrated sugar 
producers, the Company’s 10 
manufacturing facilities and 80,000 
TCD crushing capacity enable an 
efficient, diversified value chain 
spanning sugar, ethanol, and 
renewable power.
The Company built a robust, 
integrated manufacturing ecosystem 
spanning sugar, ethanol, and value-
added products — designed to 
maximise efficiency, ensure flexibility,

realities.
The Company’s principal 
manufacturing competence lies in 
its multi-feedstock and multi-product 
flexibility. Its facilities are equipped to 
switch between operational modes 
Syrup, B-Heavy, C-Heavy, as well as

advantage. The Company 
has progressively invested in 
distillation capacities and process 
configurations that allow the 
dynamic diversion between 
sugar and ethanol. Balrampur’s 
manufacturing strength lies not in 
scale alone; it lies in its ability to 
convert flexibility into profitability

feedstock architecture enables the 
Company to respond dynamically to 
policy shifts, pricing signals, and cane 
availability—transforming operational 
agility into sustained margin 
resilience.

manufactured capital is was 
anchored in multiple core principles:
Integration: Comprised the use of 
one end product (manufactured 
within) as a raw material for the 
manufacture of another product, 
widening the value chain and 
enhancing resource utilisation and 
moderating carbon footprint.
Asset optimisation: Comprised 
initiatives to maximise capacity 
utilisation, reduce downtime, 
and enhance throughput 
(through preventive maintenance, 
debottlenecking, and structured 
monitoring systems).
Process excellence: Comprised 
advanced technologies and process 
controls to improve extraction 
efficiency, reduce losses, and sustain 
product quality across production 
batches and units.

integration of energy-efficient 
systems, emission reduction

Technologies: Comprised the 
early adoption of cutting-edge 
and energy-efficient technologies 
(including advanced evaporation 
systems, bagasse dryers, and air 
pollution control solutions such as 
wet electrostatic precipitators).

How we enhanced our mill blower reliability through systemic improvements
Case study
The Electrical Engineering team 
conducted a detailed analysis 
and identified inadequate bearing 
capacity and insufficient cooling as 
the primary causes of failure.
Challenge: Reliable operation 
of mill blowers is essential for 
uninterrupted crushing operations. 
However, frequent bearing failures 
in the mill blowers at Balrampur’s 
Rauzagaon Chini Mills (RCM) and 
Haidergarh Chini Mills (HCM) units 
caused repeated breakdowns.
Kaizen implementation: A two-
pronged engineering solution 
was implemented: The existing 
6206 bearing was upgraded to a 
higher-capacity 6309 bearing to 
improve load-handling capability 
and operational reliability. The 
blower cooler arrangement 
was strengthened to enhance 
heat dissipation and maintain 
lower operating temperatures. 
These modifications improved 
the mechanical and thermal 
performance of the blower system.
Results: There was a significant 
reduction in recurring bearing 
failures. Blower stability improved. 
Equipment availability enhanced 
during the crushing season. 
Breakdown-related stoppages 
and maintenance interventions 
declined. Operations became safer.

How we enhanced 33 KV VCB reliability through dual power source 
provision for spring charging
Case study
Kaizen type: B-Type (Cross-
functional / Electrical 
Infrastructure)
Background: The 33 KV Vacuum 
Circuit Breaker (VCB) installed 
in the switchyard is a critical 
component of the plant’s power 
distribution network. During off-
season maintenance, frequent grid 
disturbances resulted in prolonged 
power outages.
Each time the breaker operated 
during a fault condition, its spring 
mechanism discharged and 
required recharging before the 
breaker could be operated again. 
However, the spring charge motor 
was connected only to the raw 
power supply. Whenever the grid 
supply failed, the motor could 
not recharge the spring, delaying 
breaker restoration and impacting 
maintenance activities.
Problem statement: The spring 
charge motor depended entirely 
on a single power source. During 
power failures, the spring could 
not be recharged, preventing 
timely operation of the breaker 
even after the grid fault had been 
cleared. This reduced switchyard 
reliability and increased restoration 
time.
Root cause analysis: A detailed 
review revealed that the spring 
charge motor was connected 
only to the raw 230 V AC supply. 
No alternate power source 
was available to recharge the 
breaker spring during grid failure 
conditions, resulting in delayed 
breaker readiness and restoration.
Improvement: To overcome 
this limitation, the Electrical 
team provided Raw Supply and 
UPS Supply (230 V AC) to the 
spring charge motor through a 
changeover switch.
The modification created a dual 
power source arrangement, 
ensuring that the spring charging 
mechanism remained functional 
even when raw supply was 
unavailable. This enabled the 
breaker to remain ready for 
operation during grid disturbances 
and restoration activities.
Outcome: The improvement 
enhanced the reliability and 
availability of the 33 KV VCB 
system. Breaker operation 
became possible even during 
raw supply failures, resulting in a 
faster restoration following grid 
disturbances.
The initiative also reduced 
dependence on DG sets during 
restoration activities, leading to 
lower fuel consumption and 
operating costs. In addition, it 
improved safety by reducing 
operator fatigue, minimizing 
emergency intervention 
requirements and enabling 
smoother handling of fault 
conditions.

Challenges and responses
The shift from reactive crop 
management to predictive precision 
agriculture is a massive operational 
leap. By treating cane cultivation as 
a data-driven matrix rather than a set 
of isolated variables, one is changing 
the efficiency of the supply chain 
right at the source.
Here is why developing this capability 
is a strong strategic move:
Moving from reactive to 
predictive
Closing the yield gap: Identifying 
the delta between a farm 
pocket's potential and its actual 
performance allows one to stop 
treating underperformance as an 
environmental inevitability and start 
treating it as a solvable mismatch of 
inputs.
Targeted deployment: Matching 
specific cane varieties to granular soil 
profiles and precipitation patterns 
moves cultivation away from a ‘one 
size fits all’ approach. This reduces 
crop failure risk and maximizes the 
return on agricultural inputs.
Stabilizing quality: By controlling for 
the variables of temperature and soil, 
one can better predict and stabilize 
the sucrose content and overall 
quality of the harvest before it ever 
reaches the factory gates.
The broader economic 
impact
This level of farm-side optimization 
does more than just help the 
growers; it impacts downstream 
viability.
When navigating the rising statutory 
costs of raw materials, maximizing 
the per-acre yield and the inherent 
juice quality provides a financial 
buffer. A stable, high-quality cane 
supply is exactly what allows a mill 
to operate efficiently, absorb pricing 
pressures, and confidently manage 
the diversion of excess sugarcane or 
B-heavy molasses toward meeting 
national ethanol blending targets.

How we drove steam economy and bagasse savings 
through process optimisation - Kumbhi Unit
Case study
Background
With the ongoing commissioning 
of the PLA cogeneration boiler, 
enhancing bagasse availability 
became a priority. The unit 
identified an opportunity to 
improve steam economy across 
the process house, reducing steam 
consumption per tonne of cane 
crushed and increasing bagasse 
availability for power generation.
Challenge
Steam consumption across the 
heating, evaporation and boiling 
stations limited the quantity 
of bagasse available for the 
cogeneration boiler. The objective 
was to maximise steam utilisation, 
recover energy losses and optimise 
process operations to achieve 
sustainable bagasse savings.
Improvements
Heating, evaporation and boiling 
operations were optimised through 
condensate recovery, enhanced 
vapour utilisation and equipment 
upgrades. 
Key interventions included heater 
modifications, split calandria 
implementation, commissioning 
of three 4,500 m² Falling Film 
Evaporators, five honeycomb 
calandria batch pans and two 38 
TPH bagasse dryers, improving 
process efficiency, steam economy 
and plant performance.
Resource optimisation
The integrated approach ensured 
the maximum utilisation of 
available energy while reducing 
overall steam demand.
Results
The project reduced steam 
consumption from 36.96% on cane 
in SS 24-25 to 32.95% on cane in 
SS 25-26. The initiative delivered 
steam savings of ~65,000 tonnes. 
Based on a steam-to-fuel ratio of 
2.55, the unit achieved bagasse 
savings of ~25,000 tonnes. The 
cumulative financial benefit: ~H750 
lakh.

Inflation remained low throughout

CPI inflation estimated at 2.1%, well 
below the Reserve Bank of India's 
medium-term target of 4%. The 
favourable inflation environment 
enabled the RBI to reduce the policy

points since February 2025, while 
also providing ample liquidity support 
through CRR cuts, open market 
operations and forex swaps, thereby 
supporting domestic consumption, 
investment and credit growth.
Despite a stable domestic 
macroeconomic environment, 
the Indian rupee remained under 
pressure from external factors. 
During FY 25-26, the currency 
depreciated by around 10% against 
the US dollar. The depreciation was 
primarily driven by sustained US 
dollar strength, foreign portfolio 
outflows, elevated geopolitical 
tensions, and global trade 
uncertainties, although India's 
external sector fundamentals and 
foreign exchange reserves remained 
relatively resilient.

cautious during FY 25-26 amid 
heightened global uncertainty. 
Foreign Portfolio Investors 
(FPIs) remained net sellers, 
withdrawing a record H1.8 trillion 
from Indian equities. However, 
robust participation by Domestic 
Institutional Investors (DIIs), with 
net investments of over H8 trillion, 
provided a strong counterbalance, 
underscoring the increasing depth, 
resilience, and maturity of India's 
domestic capital markets.

a broad-based correction during 
FY 25-26. The BSE Sensex closed 
5.36% lower than its level a year 
earlier. Similarly, the Nifty 50 declined 
3.6%. The correction was primarily 
driven by heightened geopolitical 
tensions in West Asia, concerns 
over potential changes in U.S. trade 
policy, persistent global economic 
uncertainty, and sustained foreign 
portfolio outflows.

Indian sugar sector review
The global sugar market is expected 
to remain relatively balanced in 
FY 2026, with market conditions 
influenced by production prospects 
in major producing countries, 
weather patterns, currency 
movements and evolving trade 
policies. Global sugar production 
is projected to be around 181-189 
MMT in 2025-26. The increase in 
production is expected to improve 
global availability and rebuild 
inventories, although the market 
remains vulnerable to weather-
related disruptions in major 
producing regions.
Demand for sugar is expected to 
continue growing steadily, supported 
by population growth, urbanisation 
and rising consumption in emerging 
markets. However, comparatively 
higher production and improving 
stock levels could limit sustained 
upward movement in international 
sugar prices. Brazil is likely to remain 
the dominant exporter, while 
developments in India will continue 
to have a significant bearing on 
global trade flows and prices. Going 
forward, weather conditions, ethanol 
diversion, crude oil prices, exchange-
rate movements and government 
trade policies will remain key 
determinants of the global sugar 
balance.
Performance of major sugar 
producing countries
Brazil: Sugar production in Brazil 
is expected to increase marginally 
to ~40.4 MMT compared to ~40.2 
MMT in the previous season. CS mills 
directed 50.7–51% of cane to sugar 
— the highest mix in several years 
— as international prices favoured 
sweetener over ethanol for much of 
the season. Higher availability of corn 
ethanol could reduce dependence 
on sugarcane based ethanol, thereby 
limiting sucrose diversion towards 
ethanol production and potentially 
supporting higher sugar availability 
with a favourable shift in sugar mix.
European Union: Production is 
expected to decrease to ~17.0 
MMT compared to ~17.8 MMT in 
the previous season due to decline 
in sugar beet area, particularly in 
France and Germany. Consumption 
and stocks are largely unchanged. 
Imports are expected to increase, 
while exports decline.
Thailand: Production stood at ~11.4 
million tonnes as compared to ~11.0 
million tonnes on higher cane output 
and yields. With consumption flat, 
exports are projected to rebound to 
7.0 million tonnes, reducing stocks to 
10.0 million tonnes.
India: Gross sugar production (pre-
diversion to Ethanol) is estimated 
to be ~31.0 million tonnes, 
driven by favourable weather, 
expanded planting and improved 
yields following El Nino impacts. 
Consumption is expected to rise.
Pakistan: Production is expected 
at 6.6 MMT compared to 6.8 
MMT in previous year supported 
by expanded harvested area and 
improved irrigation infrastructure.
China: Production is forecasted at 
~11.5 MMT up from ~11.2 MMT in the 
previous season. This is supported 
by favourable weather in Guangxi 
and Yunnan provinces. Despite rising 
domestic output, China retains a 
structural annual deficit of 5–6 MMT, 
sustaining 4.6–5.3 MMT of sugar 
imports and anchoring global trade 
flows.
India’s sugar sector is currently 
navigating a tight supply 
environment, shifting policy controls 
on exports, and balancing the dual 
demands of food security versus 
biofuel blending. Key factors include 
restricted exports and tight domestic 
inventories.

area under cane is low. Area

Growers are encouraged to maximise area under cane by ensuring a) timely payment b) 
timely procurement of sugarcane c) better relationship with farmers by way of village & factory 
meetings d) providing them all technical help required e) regularly working on ways to improve 
crop yield including finding new high yield future varieties. f) helping farmers in time of need.
Cane availability is lower if 
the yield of sugarcane is low. 
Rainfall impacts cane yield 
a lot. Cane yield is adversely 
impacted if rainfall is not timely 
and if rainfall is heavy within 
short span of time.
Growers are having irrigation resources which are used when the required rainfall is not there. 
In cane areas where the water drainage is not there & where there is water stagnation, growers 
are advised to keep varieties like CoLK 94184 which can perform even on plots with flood water. 
Further, every year it is ensured that proper desilting & cleaning of all water bodies & drainage 
areas is done.
High Temperature during 
summer adversely impacts cane 
yield
Growers are advised to do irrigation based on requirement of field preferably in a span of every 
seven to ten days during summer.
Higher cane availability requires 
varieties which gives high yield. 
High Yielding variety Co-0238 
area very low now due to red 
rot disease. No matching variety 
available till date to match this 
variety.
Older variety Co 118 yield is very good. Yield of new variety Co 15023 is also very good but it 
requires proper care. Yield of CoLK 14201 is also good but it requires timely planting. Further out 
of more than 50 new varieties under trial, we have already shortlisted five varieties which will be 
further reviewed closely before commercial planting.
Cane availability is lower if there 
is high incidence of insect, 
pests & diseases.
Insect, pests & diseases are controlled mechanically after several rounds of screening of each 
plot.
Cane Yield is lower if the cane 
planting is not done timely.
Growers are educated the financial benefits of doing timely planting. Early & late planting varieties 
are also advised to growers to get better yield.
Cane availability is lower if 
there is diversion of sugar cane 
to nearby units of other sugar 
factories or cane being supplied 
to kohlu & crushers which 
sometimes pay more price of 
sugarcane than SAP.
Diversion of sugarcane is minimised to other places by a) timely payment b) better arrangements 
of transport & labour c) proper indent management d) education to growers on importance of 
maintaining basic quota. e) maintaining personal relationship with each farmer.
Cane availability is lower due 
to attack of sugarcane by stray

II. Sugar Recovery Risk
Sugar Recovery is mainly 
dependent on the varietal 
balance. If the sugar unit has 
higher proportion of high 
sugared variety, its recovery will 
be more. Due to incidence of 
red rot in high sugared Co 0238 
variety, area under this variety 
has reduced. No matching 
variety with sizeable area 
available till date to match this 
variety.
Recovery of older variety Co 118 with sizeable cane area is at par with Co 0238 variety. Recovery 
of new variety Co 15023 is better than Co 0238 but it is under adoptation stage & its area will 
rise gradually. Recovery of CoLK 14201 is also good. Further out of more than 50 new varieties 
under trial, we have already shortlisted five varieties which will be further reviewed closely before 
commercial planting. Their trial result shows good recovery.
Higher sugar recovery requires 
healthy cane & cane free 
from insect, pests & disease. 
Recovery of sugarcane 
impacted by insect, pests & 
disease is lower & it can go very 
down depending on the nature 
& quantum of incidence.
Insect, pests & diseases are controlled mechanically after several rounds of screening of each 
plot. We also take help of specialised scientists who visits our factories frequently & help us 
identifying these at an early stage & suggest us timely remedial action.
Time lag between harvesting of 
sugar cane at growers field to 
crushing of sugarcane at plant 
also impacts sugar recovery.
In order to achieve minimum cut to crush time, we ensure the following: a) Supply tickets to 
growers are given timely so that they have sufficient time for harvesting & their supply is not failed 
since there is a timeline for supply. b) help growers in providing them harvesting labour if there 
is shortage c) convince growers to reduce time of harvesting by engaging more labour keeping 
the mandays required same for harvesting d) ensure sufficient vehicles are available with growers 
for bringing cane to centre / gate from field e) proper arrangements of labour & transport at cane 
purchasing centres.
Sugar Recovery is reduced if 
the extraneous matter in cane 
is high.
Better cane quality with lower extraneous matter is achieved by : a) engaging with growers 
through out the year for supplying fresh & clean cane b) Checking cane quality at the point of 
harvesting c) Strict checking at factory gate & centre by our team & returning cane whose quality 
is below standard d) Giving reward to growers bringing best quality cane every day
Sugar recovery is low if the 
ratoon cane crushing is 
completed earlier & plant cane 
arrives before time for crushing 
when it is not fully matured.
Factory start date is arrived at after considering the timely arrival of plant cane. Sometimes 
growers are also asked to delay supply of unmatured cane.
Rainfall & climate plays a 
very important role in sugar 
recovery as detailed below: a) 
extreme temperatures, both 
high and low, reduces sugar 
recovery b) excessive rainfall, 
especially during the maturity 
period, reduces sugar recovery 
c) strong winds and extreme 
weather events like cyclones 
can damage sugarcane plants 
by lodging which reduces sugar 
recovery.
Impact of climatic conditions on sugar recovery is minimised to the extent possible by a) 
identifying cane area where the impact is less & purchasing more cane from that area to the 
extent possible although there are government rules for calendaring & purchase which limit this 
activity b) advance planning for desilting & cleaning of water bodies & arrangement of irrigation 
facilities for growers to address excess / short rainfall c) advance planning for repropping of 
lodged cane within 3-4 days of lodging.

Industry Scenario and Outlook
Sugar
India began the sugar season 2025-26 (October to 
September) with an opening inventory of around 5.00 
MMT (Metric Million Tonnes). Gross sugar production for 
the season 2025-26 is estimated at 31 MMT, compared 
to 29.5 MMT in previous season, which represented an 
increase of ~1.5 MMT (~6%). There was a sugar diversion 
towards ethanol in season 2025-26 that is estimated at ~3 
MMT as compared to ~3.4 MMT in the previous season. 
Net sugar production for the season 2025-26 is estimated 
at ~28.0 MMT, compared with the previous season’s 
production of 26.1 MMT.
The government permitted the export of 1.58 MMT sugar 
during sugar season 2025-26. It is expected that out of the 
export quota ~0.70 MMT would be exported considering 
the ongoing West Asia crisis leading to disruptions in trade 
and increased freight costs. The domestic demand for 
sugar is expected to be ~28 MMT, compared to 28.10 
MMT in the previous season.
As a result, India’s carry forward sugar stock as on 30th 
September 2026 is expected to be ~4.30 MMT. In the 
upcoming sugar season sugar mills are likely to start early, this 
stock level should not pose as an issue for the Government.
Domestic sugar prices for UP-based millers ranged 
between H39.00 and H41.50 per kg during the year ended 
March, 2026. Export allowed by Government has helped 
in arresting the downward slide in the domestic sugar 
prices. Ex-mill sugar prices in state of Uttar Pradesh were 
~H41.50/kg at the time of writing this report.
Ethanol
The Indian government implemented the ethanol blending 
programme (EBP), wherein oil marketing companies 
(OMCs) marketed petrol blended with ethanol as per BIS 
specifications. The government targeted 20% ethanol 
blending with petrol by 2025-26 and 30% by 2030.
Since 2014-15, the government adopted the ethanol 
pricing mechanism linked to fair and remunerative price 
(FRP) of sugarcane. It mandated that ethanol prices, 
whether higher or lower than petrol, would be adjusted 
by oil marketing companies in the retail petrol price with a 
full pass-through to consumers, ensuring that the pricing 
mechanism would not be linked to crude prices. As a result, 
over the years the industry invested around H40,000 crore 
(encouraged by policy measures) for ethanol production 
through diverse sugar feedstock.
For the ethanol year 2023-24, 2024-25 and 2025-26 no 
increase in ethanol prices was announced for the juice/
B-heavy route ethanol in spite of increase in the FRP of 
sugarcane by ~16.4% from H305 per quintal to H355 per 
quintal. The sugar sector represented the backbone of the 
ambitious EBP since inception, contributing over 80% of 
supplies up to 2021-22 ESY. Thereafter the share of sugar 
sector in supply of Ethanol to OMC’s have come down 
drastically every single year in the wake of no revision in 
Ethanol prices.
Further the FRP for the sugar season 2026-27 has been 
increased to H365 per quintal an increase of H10 per quintal.

180 | Balrampur Chini Mills Limited
The production of ethanol from juice and B-heavy 
molasses requires a sugar sacrifice that needs to be 
compensated by an ethanol price sufficient to cover the 
value of sugar sacrificed. A formula-based approach needs 
to be reinstated to determine price of ethanol after taking 
into consideration the increase in sugar production cost 
due to an upward revision in the FRP of sugarcane as per 
the past practice. Infact CACP has also recommended for 
revising the sugarcane based Ethanol procurement prices.
If the correct ethanol realisation is not fixed, this could 
damage the fabric of the industry leading to the following:
	
Lower diversion of sugar towards ethanol
	
Build-up of sugar inventory that could result in lower 
sugar realizations requiring compulsory sugar exports 
that could need financial subsidy if global prices 
are inadequate.
	
Higher sugar inventory that could lead to lower sugar 
prices, losses and delays in cane price payments 
to farmers.
Sugarcane is an efficient crop when it comes to water use 
efficiency i.e. per unit of water consumed by sugarcane 
gives the highest quantity of ethanol compared to other 
crops. Sugarcane also demonstrates superior land use 
efficiency and the lowest GHG emissions among the major 
first-generation feedstocks. A successful E20 program 
utilizing sugarcane-based ethanol can reduce tailpipe 
carbon emissions by about 30%. Life-cycle analyses show 
that ethanol from sugarcane can cut greenhouse gas 
emissions by roughly 65%, while maize-based ethanol 
provides a reduction of approximately 50%. Hon’ble Prime 
Minister has also tweeted that “Due to ethanol blending, 
we are saving the import of about 4.5 crore barrels of oil 
every year”. Sugarcane farmers get guaranteed FRP as 
determined by the Government year-on-year and relative 
gross returns are higher compared with other crops as 
agreed to by the inter-ministerial committee.
The shift from a predictable, formula-based pricing model 
to the current stagnation has essentially decoupled the 
"output" price (ethanol) from the "input" cost (sugarcane 
FRP), threatening the stability of the entire ecosystem.
Government Policies
The government sustained most policies in the sugar 
season 2025-26 as announced in previous years with the 
objective of ensuring adequate domestic sugar availability, 
supporting sugar realisations and ensuring timely farmer 
payments. These policies included the unrestricted 
diversion of sugar to ethanol and permitted sugar exports, 
except for the non-revision of ethanol prices under the 
juice and B-heavy routes for the third consecutive year.
The following policies of the government prevailed during 
the season 2025-26:
	
The fair and remunerative price (FRP) of sugarcane 
for the sugar season 2025-26 was revised to H355 
per quintal up from H340 per quintal in the previous 
season (linked to a basic recovery rate of 10.25%).
	
	The State advised price (SAP) of sugarcane for Uttar 
Pradesh was increased to H400 per quintal (for early 
maturing variety of sugarcane) from H370 per quintal 
in previous season.

	Export were permitted up to 1.587 MMT during the 
2025-26 season.
	
	Ethanol prices for the supply period from November

H65.61per BL for ethanol produced from direct cane

produced from B-heavy molasses and H57.97 per BL 
for C-heavy molasses route.
	
	The oil marketing companies decide differential prices 
for ethanol produced from damaged/ surplus food 
grains. For the supply period from November 2025 to 
October 2026, the price for ethanol from damaged

H64.00 per BL and H71.86 per BL respectively. Ethanol 
price from FCI surplus rice route was increased from

	

Our Expectations
Increase the prices of juice, B-heavy based ethanol in line 
with FRP hike, following the mechanism adopted up to 
2022-23 which considers the value of sugar sacrificed. 
The minimum selling price of sugar (as part of the policy 
framework) should be revised upwards in view of the 
increase in FRP.
The government should announce the ex-mill price 
of juice and B-heavy based ethanol prior to the tender 
process, based on the pricing mechanism adopted up to 
2022-23, linked to FRP of sugarcane and accounting for 
sugar sacrificed. This could benefit all stakeholders and 
support long-term sectorial sustainability.
By reverting to the proven pricing mechanisms of the past, 
the government can transform the sugar sector from a 
cyclical, subsidy-dependent industry into a robust, self-
sustaining energy powerhouse.

Global sugar sector review
The global sugar market is expected to remain relatively 
balanced in FY 2026, with market conditions influenced 
by production prospects in major producing countries, 
weather patterns, currency movements and evolving trade 
policies. Global sugar production is projected to be around 
181-189 MMT in 2025-26. The increase in production 
is expected to improve global availability and rebuild 
inventories, although the market remains vulnerable to 
weather-related disruptions in major producing regions.
Demand for sugar is expected to continue growing 
steadily, supported by population growth, urbanisation 
and rising consumption in emerging markets. However, 
comparatively higher production and improving stock 
levels could limit sustained upward movement in 
international sugar prices. Brazil is likely to remain the 
dominant exporter, while developments in India will 
continue to have a significant bearing on global trade flows 
and prices. Going forward, weather conditions, ethanol 
diversion, crude oil prices, exchange-rate movements and 
government trade policies will remain key determinants of 
the global sugar balance.

Investor Education and Protection Fund 
(IEPF)
Pursuant to the provisions of Section 124 of the Act, Investor 
Education and Protection Fund Authority (Accounting, 
Audit, Transfer and Refund) Rules, 2016 (“IEPF Rules”) read 
with the relevant circulars and amendments thereto, the 
amount of dividend remaining unpaid or unclaimed for a 
period of seven years from the due date is required to be 
transferred to the Investor Education and Protection Fund 
(“IEPF”), constituted by the Central Government.
Further, pursuant to the provisions of IEPF Rules, all shares 
in respect of which any dividend which has not been paid 
or claimed for seven consecutive years shall be transferred 
by the Company to the designated Demat Account of the 
IEPF Authority (‘IEPF Account’) within a period of thirty 
days of such shares becoming due to be transferred to 
the IEPF Account.
The Company sends advance communication to the 
concerned shareholders at their address registered with 
the Company and publishes notices in the newspapers for 
taking appropriate action to claim unclaimed dividend and 
the shares due for transfer to IEPF.
Despite these efforts, an amount of H24.79 lakhs, being 
the unpaid and unclaimed dividend amount pertaining to 
the financial year 2018-19, was transferred to the IEPF in 
accordance with the provisions of the Act.
In terms of the IEPF Rules, the Company has also 
transferred 39,818 equity shares of face value of H1 each 
to IEPF on which dividend has not been claimed for 
seven consecutive years after following the prescribed 
procedure. Details of dividends that are due for transfer 
to IEPF for the next 7 (seven) years on their respective due 
dates, are available on the website of the Company at 
https://chini.com/investors/unpaid-dividend-iepf/.

CORPORATE GOVERNANCE REPORT
Company’s Philosophy on Code of Governance
Corporate Governance refers to, a set of laws, regulations, good practices & systems that enables an organisation to 
perform efficiently and ethically to generate long-term wealth and create value for all its stakeholders. Sound governance 
practices and responsible corporate behaviour contribute to superior long-term performance of organisations. Corporate 
Governance requires everyone to raise their level of competency and capability to meet the expectations in managing 
the enterprise and its resources optimally with prudent ethical standards.
The Company recognises that good corporate governance is a continuous exercise. Adherence to transparency, 
accountability, fairness and ethical standards are an integral part of the Company’s function. The Company’s structure, 
business dealings, administration and disclosure practices are aligned to good corporate governance philosophy. The 
Company has an adequate system of control in place to ensure that the executive decisions taken should result in 
optimum growth and development which benefits all the stakeholders. The Company also aims to increase and sustain 
its corporate values through growth and innovation.
Board of Directors
The Company recognizes the importance of a diverse Board in its success. The Board is entrusted with the ultimate 
responsibility of the management, direction and performance of the Company and has been vested with the requisite 
powers, authorities and duties. Regulation 17(1) of the SEBI (Listing Obligations and Disclosure Requirements) Regulations, 
2015 (as amended) (the “Listing Regulations”) mandates a Company which does not have a regular non-executive 
chairperson to have at least half of the Board of Directors to be comprised of Independent Directors. As on 31st March, 
2026, the Board comprised of 7 (seven) directors, of which 4 (four) were Independent Directors. The composition of the 
Board is in conformity with the requirements of Regulation 17(1) of the Listing Regulations.
